content: For long-term storage exceeding one year, stool samples should be kept at a temperature of -70°C. Storing samples at -20°C for extended periods can lead to a decline in the ability to characterize rotaviruses. If stool samples are intended for testing bacterial or parasitic pathogens using conventional methods, they must be transported to the laboratory within two hours of collection and placed on appropriate media. Subsequently, these samples should be stored at -20°C or lower until testing is performed. Laboratory confirmation is essential for diagnosing rotavirus gastroenteritis. Various diagnostic tests are commercially available. Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) are widely used to detect rotavirus antigens directly in stool specimens. Examples of EIA kits include Premier™ Rotaclone®, ProSpecT™, and RIDASCREEN®. The sensitivity of EIAs ranges from 75% to 82%, with a specificity of 100%. However, false negatives may occur, particularly at lower viral loads, though the clinical significance of rotavirus at concentrations below the EIA detection threshold remains unclear. Latex agglutination assays are rapid and simple immunochromatographic test strips but are generally less sensitive and specific compared to EIAs. Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is employed to characterize rotavirus strains and identify both G and P genotypes. A subset of rotavirus-positive stool samples obtained from routine surveillance should be selected for strain characterization. It is recommended that a minimum of 50–60 randomly selected specimens be genotyped annually per country, with the selection proportional to the age and seasonal distribution of cases. If resources allow, all EIA-positive samples should undergo strain characterization. Only specimens larger than 3 mL should be chosen to ensure sufficient material for testing. Non-typeable isolates should be sent to a reference laboratory for sequencing. A suspected case of rotavirus gastroenteritis refers to a child under five years of age admitted to a hospital ward or emergency unit for treatment of acute watery diarrhea (lasting less than 14 days), defined as three or more loose or watery stools within a 24-hour period. Cases involving bloody diarrhea or nosocomial infections are excluded. A confirmed case is a suspected case in which rotavirus presence is demonstrated in stool using EIA or PCR-based methods. Routine contact tracing is not conducted for rotavirus. Currently, there is no specific antiviral therapy available for rotavirus infections. Fluid replacement is critical to prevent or treat dehydration. Low-osmolarity oral rehydration salts (ORS) are more effective than conventional ORS formulations for fluid replacement. If ORS is unavailable, appropriate fluids available at home can be used. Zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea episodes, stool volume, and the need for advanced medical care. Continued feeding, including breastfeeding, is strongly recommended. Country-specific guidelines or Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines should be followed for managing rotavirus cases. Rotavirus is an endemic disease and does not typically result in large-scale outbreaks requiring intervention. Diarrhea caused by other pathogens, such as norovirus, cholera, or enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC), may occur during outbreaks. Syndromic surveillance for diarrhea may detect such outbreaks, but sentinel surveillance is not sufficient for this purpose. Laboratory capacity developed for rotavirus surveillance can potentially be expanded to identify outbreaks of diarrhea caused by other pathogens. A previously available rotavirus vaccine was associated with an increased risk of intussusception. Surveillance for intussusception in some countries is important to monitor the safety of rotavirus vaccines after their introduction. However, the absence of such surveillance should not delay the introduction of rotavirus vaccines. Sentinel surveillance sites used for rotavirus can also be considered for intussusception surveillance and for monitoring other enteric pathogens, such as ETEC, Shigella, and norovirus, for which vaccines are in development. These considerations may require modifications in surveillance approaches, including case definitions, tests performed, and case investigation forms. The number of rotavirus cases occurring each month should be reported to the Ministry of Health. If no diarrhea cases are identified at a sentinel site, this should be explicitly indicated in the report (zero reporting). Aggregate reporting (numbers only) is sufficient for routine reporting, even if case-based surveillance is conducted. There are no global reporting requirements for rotavirus. Each suspected case should be assigned a unique identification number. Data should be periodically analyzed to understand disease characteristics and monitor the surveillance system. Age distribution and seasonality are important in the epidemiology of rotavirus gastroenteritis. Suspected and confirmed cases should be described by the epidemiological week of diarrhea onset, and data must be consolidated monthly by the age of affected children and the location of cases. It should also be determined whether the case is isolated or part of an outbreak in a daycare center, institution, or community. Minimal data analysis should include the number of hospitalizations, the percentage of diarrhea-associated hospitalizations caused by rotavirus by age group, and the number of deaths associated with rotavirus diarrhea. Enhanced analyses may include clinical and epidemiological characteristics of cases, genotype distribution, seasonal trends, and the peak of rotavirus activity. For population-based surveillance, rates of hospitalization and deaths associated with diarrhea and rotavirus per 1,000 children under five years of age per year should be recorded. Rotavirus surveillance data are primarily used to support national vaccination strategies. Rotavirus is not targeted for global elimination or eradication. The impact of vaccines can be evaluated by comparing annual rates of rotavirus disease before and after vaccine introduction. Indirect effects of vaccination can be estimated by monitoring reductions in diarrhea and rotavirus rates among unvaccinated children. Vaccine effectiveness can be assessed through test-negative, case-control studies, where confirmed rotavirus cases serve as cases and rotavirus-negative gastroenteritis cases serve as controls. This design minimizes selection bias, as all children are enrolled prospectively before confirmation of rotavirus infection or vaccination status. However, documenting vaccination status requires significant effort. Rotavirus is an RNA virus with seven known groups (A to G). Group A is responsible for most human illnesses and is classified into G and P genotypes. The most common genotypes infecting humans include G1P[8], G2P[4], G3P[8], G4P[8], G9P[8], and G12 in combination with P[6] or P[8]. Rotavirus primarily affects infants aged 3 months to 1 year and is the leading cause of severe diarrheal disease in young children worldwide. Most rotavirus deaths occur in less developed countries due to limited access to timely healthcare. In low-income countries, the disease may be more severe due to concurrent infections, malnutrition, and other factors. Year-round transmission due to climatic factors may also contribute to the higher disease burden in these regions. In high-income countries, rotavirus accounted for 40–50% of hospital admissions for diarrhea in the pre-vaccine era. Rotavirus belongs to the Reoviridae family. Its reservoir is the gastrointestinal tract and stool of infected humans. Although rotavirus infections occur in other mammals, animal-to-human transmission is rare and unlikely to cause clinical illness. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route.
